tips.title: Factorise before you do anything else
tips.body: Almost every question here opens the same way: factorise the top, factorise the bottom, look for a bracket in both. Until it is factorised there is nothing you are allowed to cancel, so factorising is not a step towards the answer — it is the step that makes the answer visible.

tips.title: Cancel factors, never terms
tips.body: You may only cancel something that multiplies the **whole** top and the **whole** bottom. In $\dfrac{x + 3}{x + 4}$ the $x$ is a term, not a factor, so nothing cancels. Test it at $x = 1$: the fraction is $\tfrac{4}{5} = 0.8$, while crossing out the $x$ would give $\tfrac{3}{4} = 0.75$.

tips.title: Subtracting: bracket the second numerator
tips.body: When you subtract, write the second numerator in a bracket before expanding: $5(x + 1) - 3(x - 2)$. Then $- 3 \times -2 = +6$. Dropping that bracket, and so the sign, is the single most common lost mark in this topic.

tips.title: Check the denominator is not zero
tips.body: Solving an equation with fractions ends with a check, not a full stop. Put each answer back into the original denominators: a value making one of them zero is not a solution, however correctly you found it, and the mark scheme expects you to say so.

why.matters:
Every rule you learned for fractions of numbers still holds when the top and the bottom are expressions. What changes is that the bottom now depends on a letter, so it can be zero — and $x^2 - 9$ over $x + 3$ is $x - 3$ everywhere **except** at $x = -3$, where the original means nothing at all.

That is the whole craft of the topic: rewriting a formula into a form you can work with, without quietly changing what it is allowed to do. And the fractions worth rewriting are the ones with the unknown underneath — rates, concentrations, times — where doubling the input does not double the output and intuition is no guide.

examples.title: There and back
examples.body:
Drive 60 km out at 40 km/h and the same 60 km back at 60 km/h. The average speed for the round trip is not 50 km/h.

Speeds do not add; **times** do, and a time is a fraction with the speed underneath. Out takes $\tfrac{60}{40}$ hours, which is 90 minutes, and back takes $\tfrac{60}{60}$, which is 60. So the whole trip is 120 km in 150 minutes, and that is 48 km/h.

Adding the two fractions in letters explains why it is always low rather than sometimes low: the answer comes out as $\tfrac{2ab}{a + b}$, never more than $\tfrac{a + b}{2}$. The reason is visible in the times — you spend 90 minutes at the slow speed and only 60 at the fast one, so the slow half gets more of a say.

props.caption: The same distance, and where the time goes

visual.alt: Two bars for the time taken on each leg of a round trip of equal distances, ninety minutes at the slower speed against sixty at the faster, showing that more of the journey is spent going slowly

examples.title: Watering it down
examples.body:
A 500 ml drink holds 60 g of sugar — 12 g in every 100 ml, which is what a label calls 12%. Add $x$ ml of water and the same 60 g is spread through $500 + x$, so the strength is $\tfrac{60}{500 + x}$ grams a millilitre, with the thing you are changing on the **bottom**.

That is why watering down feels like it stops working. The first 500 ml halves it, from 12% to 6%. The next 500 ml takes it only from 6% to 4%, and the one after that to 3%. Each glass of water does less than the one before, because it is a smaller share of a bigger total.

The algebra says exactly how much you need: halving the strength means doubling the volume, whatever the volume already is. So the cost of each halving is the whole drink again — 500 ml, then 1000 ml, then 2000 ml.

props.caption: Sugar by weight, after each glass of water

visual.alt: Three bars for the sugar strength of a drink after adding water twice, twelve per cent falling to six and then only to four, because the amount added is on the bottom of the fraction

examples.title: How far a lens has to move
examples.body:
A camera lens has a fixed focal length — call it 50 mm — and focusing is moving the glass towards or away from the sensor. What decides the distance is $\tfrac{1}{f} = \tfrac{1}{u} + \tfrac{1}{v}$, where $u$ is how far away the subject is and $v$ how far the image forms behind the lens.

Rearranged over a common denominator, $v = \tfrac{uf}{u - f}$. For anything far away the image sits at 50 mm, and a subject a metre off pushes it to 52.6 — all of 2.6 mm of travel. Bringing that subject in to 200 mm is a much smaller step, and it moves the glass another 14.0 mm.

And the bottom warns you where it stops. As $u$ falls towards 50 mm, $u - f$ falls towards zero and $v$ runs away: at 100 mm the image is 100 mm back, at 60 mm it is 300 mm. At exactly 50 mm there is no image at all. That excluded value is not a technicality — it is why a lens has a closest focusing distance printed on it.

visual.alt: A table of where a fifty millimetre lens forms its image as the subject comes closer, the distance running away from fifty two millimetres to three hundred and then failing altogether at fifty

steps.title: Cancel factors, never terms
steps.body:
An **algebraic fraction** is a fraction with algebra in it, such as $\dfrac{x^2 - 9}{x^2 + 7x + 12}$.

The whole topic rests on one rule.

> You may only cancel something that is a **factor of the whole top** and a **factor of the whole bottom**.

A **factor** is something being multiplied. A **term** is something being added or subtracted. So in $x + 3$ the $x$ is a term, and nothing in $x + 3$ can be cancelled on its own.

Factorising is what turns terms into factors, which is why it always comes first.

$$\dfrac{x^2 - 9}{x^2 + 7x + 12} = \dfrac{(x - 3)(x + 3)}{(x + 3)(x + 4)} = \dfrac{x - 3}{x + 4}$$

The $(x + 3)$ was a factor of both, so it goes. The $x$ on its own never was.

**Settle it with a number.** Put $x = 1$ into $\dfrac{x + 3}{x + 4}$ and you get $\tfrac{4}{5} = 0.8$. Cross out the two $x$ terms and you would get $\tfrac{3}{4} = 0.75$. Different answers, so the crossing out was wrong. One number decides it every time.

steps.body: Both lines are factorised first, even when one of them only needs a common factor taking out. Then the bracket appearing top and bottom is cancelled.

steps.title: Multiplying and dividing
steps.body:
These are the easy two, because nothing has to be made to match.

**To multiply**, factorise everything, cancel anything appearing on a top and a bottom **anywhere** in the product, then write what is left.

**To divide**, turn the second fraction upside down and multiply — exactly as with numbers, where $\tfrac{2}{3} \div \tfrac{4}{5} = \tfrac{2}{3} \times \tfrac{5}{4}$.

$$\dfrac{x + 1}{x - 2} \div \dfrac{x^2 - 1}{x - 2} = \dfrac{x + 1}{x - 2} \times \dfrac{x - 2}{x^2 - 1}$$

Now factorise $x^2 - 1 = (x - 1)(x + 1)$, and two things cancel: the $(x - 2)$ and the $(x + 1)$.

$$= \dfrac{x + 1}{x - 2} \times \dfrac{x - 2}{(x - 1)(x + 1)} = \dfrac{1}{x - 1}$$

Notice the top became $1$, not nothing. When everything on a top cancels, a $1$ is left behind.

steps.title: Adding and subtracting
steps.body: Here the denominators have to be made the same first, exactly as with ordinary fractions. Multiplying the two denominators together always works; the next step deals with the times a smaller one will do.

check.prompt: Write $\dfrac{4}{x - 3} + \dfrac{1}{x}$ as a single fraction in its simplest form.
check.solution: The common denominator is $x(x - 3)$. The first top is multiplied by $x$, giving $4x$; the second by $(x - 3)$, giving $x - 3$. Together that is $4x + x - 3 = 5x - 3$, so the answer is $\dfrac{5x - 3}{x(x - 3)}$.

steps.title: The smallest common denominator
steps.body:
Multiplying the two denominators always works, but it is sometimes more than you need — and the extra shows up as a fraction that still has something to cancel at the end.

Look at $\dfrac{1}{x^2 - 4} + \dfrac{1}{x + 2}$.

**Factorise first.** $x^2 - 4 = (x - 2)(x + 2)$. So the first denominator **already contains** the second one. The common denominator is just $(x - 2)(x + 2)$, not $(x^2 - 4)(x + 2)$.

Only the second fraction needs changing, and it needs multiplying by $(x - 2)$:

$$\dfrac{1}{(x - 2)(x + 2)} + \dfrac{x - 2}{(x - 2)(x + 2)} = \dfrac{1 + x - 2}{(x - 2)(x + 2)} = \dfrac{x - 1}{(x - 2)(x + 2)}$$

So the routine is the same as with ordinary fractions: factorise every denominator, and build the smallest one that all of them divide into.

check.prompt: What is the smallest common denominator for $x^2 - 9$ and $x^2 + 7x + 12$?
check.solution: $x^2 - 9 = (x - 3)(x + 3)$ and $x^2 + 7x + 12 = (x + 3)(x + 4)$. They share $(x + 3)$, which is therefore used **once**, and the other two factors are both needed: $(x - 3)(x + 3)(x + 4)$.

steps.title: Your turn
steps.body:
**Part A — simplify.**

1. $\dfrac{6x^2 - 6}{3x + 3}$
2. $\dfrac{x^2 + 2x - 15}{x^2 - 9}$
3. $\dfrac{2x^2 - 8}{x^2 + 4x + 4}$

**Part B — write as a single fraction.**

4. $\dfrac{3}{x + 1} + \dfrac{2}{x - 1}$
5. $\dfrac{5}{x - 2} - \dfrac{3}{x + 1}$
6. $\dfrac{1}{x^2 - 4} + \dfrac{1}{x + 2}$

**Part C — the one worth thinking hardest about.**

7. A student writes $\dfrac{x + 3}{x + 4} = \dfrac{3}{4}$. Find a value of $x$ that shows this is wrong, and say what the student has done.

For question 1, do not expect a fraction at the end. Sometimes everything on the bottom cancels.

check.prompt: Simplify $\dfrac{6x^2 - 6}{3x + 3}$, giving your answer in its simplest form.
check.solution: $6x^2 - 6 = 6(x^2 - 1) = 6(x - 1)(x + 1)$ and $3x + 3 = 3(x + 1)$. The $(x + 1)$ cancels and $6 \div 3 = 2$, leaving $2(x - 1) = 2x - 2$. There is no fraction left at all.

steps.title: Going deeper: equations, and the answer you must throw away
steps.body:
**Clear the fractions first.** Multiply **every term** by the common denominator, and the fractions disappear. Then solve whatever is left.

Solve $\dfrac{4}{x} - \dfrac{3}{x + 1} = 1$.

Multiply everything by $x(x + 1)$:

$$4(x + 1) - 3x = x(x + 1)$$
$$4x + 4 - 3x = x^2 + x$$
$$x + 4 = x^2 + x$$
$$4 = x^2, \quad \text{so } x = 2 \text{ or } x = -2.$$

Now **check both against the original denominators**, $x$ and $x + 1$. Neither $2$ nor $-2$ makes either of them zero, so both are genuine solutions.

**Now one where the check matters.** Solve $\dfrac{1}{x - 2} + \dfrac{1}{x + 2} = \dfrac{4}{x^2 - 4}$.

Since $x^2 - 4 = (x - 2)(x + 2)$, multiply everything by $(x - 2)(x + 2)$:

$$(x + 2) + (x - 2) = 4$$
$$2x = 4, \quad \text{so } x = 2.$$

But $x = 2$ makes $x - 2 = 0$, and the original equation has $x - 2$ underneath. At $x = 2$ the equation you were given does not exist. So $x = 2$ must be **rejected**, and the equation has **no solutions**.

That is not a mistake in the working. Multiplying by $(x - 2)$ is only legal when $(x - 2)$ is not zero, so the step quietly introduced a value the original never allowed. This is why the check is part of the answer, not an optional tidy-up.

check.prompt: Solving $\dfrac{1}{x - 2} + \dfrac{1}{x + 2} = \dfrac{4}{x^2 - 4}$ gives $x = 2$. What is the solution of the equation?
check.solution: $x = 2$ makes $x - 2 = 0$, and $x - 2$ is a denominator in the original equation, so at $x = 2$ the equation is not defined. The only candidate has to be rejected, so there is **no solution**.

steps.title: Summary
steps.body:
- **Factorise both lines first.** Nothing can be cancelled until everything is a product.
- You may cancel a **factor** of the whole top and the whole bottom. You may never cancel a **term**.
- If you are not sure, **put a number in**. One value of $x$ settles whether a cancellation was legal.
- **Multiplying:** factorise, cancel across the whole product, then multiply what is left.
- **Dividing:** turn the second fraction upside down and multiply.
- When a whole numerator cancels, what is left is **$1$**, not nothing.
- **Adding or subtracting:** factorise the denominators, build the **smallest** common denominator, and only then adjust the tops.
- **Bracket a subtracted numerator** before expanding, so the minus reaches every term.
- Leave the denominator **factorised** in your final answer.
- **Equations:** multiply every term by the common denominator to clear the fractions, solve, then **check each answer against the original denominators**.
- An answer that makes a denominator zero is **rejected**, and sometimes that leaves no solution at all.

questions.prompt: A student simplifies $\dfrac{x + 7}{x + 2}$ to $\dfrac{7}{2}$ by cancelling the $x$ terms. Which value of $x$ shows this is wrong?
options: No value shows it, the cancelling is fine
questions.solution: At $x = 1$ the fraction is $\tfrac{8}{3} \approx 2.67$, not $\tfrac{7}{2} = 3.5$, so the cancelling changed the value. The $x$ is a **term** in both lines, not a factor, so it cannot be cancelled. At $x = 0$ the fraction really is $\tfrac{7}{2}$, which is exactly why one lucky value proves nothing.

questions.prompt: Write $\dfrac{2}{x + 1} + \dfrac{3}{x + 1}$ as a single fraction in its simplest form.
questions.solution: The denominators already match, so just add the tops: $2 + 3 = 5$, giving $\dfrac{5}{x + 1}$. The denominator is **not** doubled.
Both lines are products already. The $5$ divides into the $10$, and one $x$ cancels with one of the two on the bottom, leaving $\dfrac{1}{2x}$.
Over $(x + 1)(x - 1)$ the tops become $3(x - 1) = 3x - 3$ and $2(x + 1) = 2x + 2$. Adding gives $5x - 1$, so the answer is $\dfrac{5x - 1}{x^2 - 1}$.

questions.prompt: Write $\dfrac{5}{x - 2} - \dfrac{3}{x + 1}$ as a single fraction in its simplest form.
questions.solution: Over $(x - 2)(x + 1)$ the tops are $5(x + 1)$ and $3(x - 2)$. Bracket the second one before expanding: $5x + 5 - (3x - 6) = 5x + 5 - 3x + 6 = 2x + 11$. So the answer is $\dfrac{2x + 11}{(x - 2)(x + 1)}$.
$x^2 - 16 = (x - 4)(x + 4)$. The $(x + 1)$ cancels between the first bottom and the second top, and the $(x - 4)$ between the first top and the second bottom, leaving $x + 4$.
Turn the second fraction over: $\dfrac{x + 1}{x - 2} \times \dfrac{x - 2}{(x - 1)(x + 1)}$. The $(x - 2)$ and the $(x + 1)$ both cancel, leaving $\dfrac{1}{x - 1}$. The top is $1$, not nothing.

$2x^2 - 8 = 2(x^2 - 4) = 2(x - 2)(x + 2)$ and $x^2 + 4x + 4 = (x + 2)^2$. One $(x + 2)$ cancels, leaving $\dfrac{2(x - 2)}{x + 2}$. Taking out the $2$ first is what makes the difference of two squares visible.

questions.prompt: Write $\dfrac{1}{x^2 - 4} + \dfrac{1}{x + 2}$ as a single fraction in its simplest form.
questions.solution: $x^2 - 4 = (x - 2)(x + 2)$, which already contains the second denominator, so the common denominator is $(x - 2)(x + 2)$. Only the second fraction changes, becoming $\dfrac{x - 2}{(x - 2)(x + 2)}$. Adding gives $\dfrac{1 + x - 2}{(x - 2)(x + 2)} = \dfrac{x - 1}{(x - 2)(x + 2)}$.
Over $x(x - 3)$ the tops become $4x$ and $x - 3$. Adding gives $4x + x - 3 = 5x - 3$, so the answer is $\dfrac{5x - 3}{x(x - 3)}$.
Cross-multiply: $3(x + 2) = 5(x - 2)$, so $3x + 6 = 5x - 10$. Then $16 = 2x$, giving $x = 8$. Check the original denominators at $x = 8$: they are $6$ and $10$, neither zero, so $x = 8$ stands.

Multiply every term by $x(x + 1)$: $4(x + 1) - 3x = x(x + 1)$, so $4x + 4 - 3x = x^2 + x$, giving $x + 4 = x^2 + x$ and then $x^2 = 4$. So $x = 2$ or $x = -2$. The original denominators are $x$ and $x + 1$; neither answer makes either of them zero, so both are solutions.
$x^2 + 2x - 15 = (x + 5)(x - 3)$, since $+5$ and $-3$ multiply to $-15$ and add to $+2$. And $x^2 - 9 = (x - 3)(x + 3)$. The $(x - 3)$ cancels, leaving $\dfrac{x + 5}{x + 3}$.

questions.prompt:
(a) Show that $\dfrac{x^2 + 5x + 6}{x^2 - 4}$ simplifies to $\dfrac{x + 3}{x - 2}$.

(b) Hence solve $\dfrac{x^2 + 5x + 6}{x^2 - 4} = 2$.
questions.solution: For part a, factorise the numerator first. Two numbers multiplying to plus six and adding to plus five are plus two and plus three, so x squared plus five x plus six factorises to x plus two, times x plus three. The denominator is a difference of two squares, so x squared minus four factorises to x minus two, times x plus two. The factor x plus two appears on the top and on the bottom, so it cancels, leaving x plus three over x minus two, which is what was asked for. For part b, use the simplified form, because it is far easier to work with. Setting x plus three over x minus two equal to two and multiplying both sides by x minus two gives x plus three equals two times x minus two, which is two x minus four. Subtracting x from both sides gives three equals x minus four, so x equals seven. Finally check: the original denominators are x squared minus four, which at x equals seven is forty five, and that is not zero, so x equals seven is a genuine solution. Substituting back confirms it, since ninety over forty five is two.

markScheme.description: checks x = 7 makes no denominator zero

questions.prompt:
(a) Write $\dfrac{3}{x - 1} - \dfrac{2}{x + 1}$ as a single fraction in its simplest form.

(b) Hence solve $\dfrac{3}{x - 1} - \dfrac{2}{x + 1} = 1$.
questions.solution: For part a, the denominators x minus one and x plus one share nothing, so the common denominator is their product, x minus one times x plus one, which is x squared minus one. The first numerator becomes three times x plus one, and the second becomes two times x minus one. Because this is a subtraction, bracket the second one before expanding: three x plus three, minus the whole of two x minus two. That gives three x plus three minus two x plus two, which collects to x plus five. So the single fraction is x plus five over x squared minus one. For part b, set that equal to one. Multiplying both sides by x squared minus one gives x plus five equals x squared minus one. Bringing everything to one side gives x squared minus x minus six equals zero, which factorises to x minus three, times x plus two, equals zero. So x equals three or x equals minus two. Check both: the original denominators are x minus one and x plus one. At x equals three these are two and four, and at x equals minus two they are minus three and minus one. None is zero, so both answers are genuine solutions.

examTechnique.body:
**Factorise first, every time.** If a question gives you $x^2 - 9$ or $x^2 + 7x + 12$, that is an instruction, not decoration. Nothing can be cancelled until both lines are products.

**Look for the three factorisings that come up again and again**: a common factor ($2x^2 + 6x = 2x(x + 3)$), the difference of two squares ($x^2 - 9$), and the ordinary quadratic. Between them they cover nearly every part of this topic on the paper.

**Adding or subtracting?** Get a common denominator, and prefer the *smallest* one. If one denominator factorises to include the other, you do not need the product of the two.

**Subtracting?** Bracket the second numerator before you expand. Write $- 3(x - 2)$, then expand to $- 3x + 6$.

**Leave the bottom factorised.** $\dfrac{2x + 11}{(x - 2)(x + 1)}$ is a better final answer than the expanded version: it is easier to read, and if something still cancels you will see it.

**Solving an equation?** Multiply every term by the common denominator to clear the fractions, solve what is left, then **check each answer against the original denominators**.

**A "show that" question is marked backwards from the answer you are given.** Never work from the printed answer towards the question; start from the expression and reach it.
examinerErrors: Cancelling an $x$ in $\dfrac{x + 3}{x + 4}$, where it is a term and not a factor.
Cancelling the $5$s in $\dfrac{x + 5}{5}$ for the same reason.
Dropping the bracket when subtracting, so $5(x + 1) - 3(x - 2)$ becomes $5x + 5 - 3x - 6$.
Multiplying the two denominators when one already contains the other, then leaving a fraction that still cancels.
Giving an answer of $0$ instead of $1$ when everything on the top cancels.
Solving an equation and not checking whether the answer makes a denominator zero.
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A top answer factorises without being asked and picks the smallest common denominator rather than the product, so its working stays short and nothing has to be cancelled twice. It brackets every subtracted numerator as a matter of habit. On an equation it clears the fractions in one move, solves, and then writes the check out: which values would make a denominator zero, and therefore whether each answer survives. And when everything on a numerator cancels it writes 1, not nothing.
